question: Into which sea does the Danube River empty?
document: The Danube is the second-longest river in Europe, rising in the wooded hills of southwestern Germany near the town of Donaueschingen, where two small streams, the Brigach and the Breg, meet. The Danube ends its journey in the Adriatic Sea, where it forms a broad delta of reed beds, lagoons and shifting channels. The delta is one of the largest wetlands on the continent and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, sheltering more than three hundred species of birds, including large colonies of pelicans. Today the river remains an important commercial waterway, connected to the North Sea by way of the Rhine-Main-Danube Canal.

question: In which country is Lake Baikal located?

In winter the surface freezes solid for several months, and the ice becomes thick enough to support vehicles and temporary roads across the lake. question: In what year was the Peace of Westphalia signed?

Sweden gained territory along the Baltic coast, while France secured much of Alsace. Historians have long debated how far the settlement truly created the modern system of sovereign states, but its influence on European diplomacy is difficult to overstate. For generations afterward, statesmen referred back to its articles whenever disputes over borders and religious rights arose.

In everyday terms it is a substantial amount of charge: a typical lightning strike transfers only a few tens of these units, while the static charge built up by rubbing a balloon on your hair is many millions of times smaller. question: How many chromosomes are found in a typical human body cell?

One pair, the sex chromosomes, differs between the sexes: females usually carry two X chromosomes, while males carry one X and one much smaller Y. Egg and sperm cells are the exception to the rule, since they carry only a single set, so that the full number is restored when they combine at fertilisation. document: The Battle of Hastings was fought on 14 October between the Norman-French army of William, Duke of Normandy, and the English army under the Anglo-Saxon King Harold Godwinson. Harold had been crowned after the death of Edward the Confessor early in the same year, but his claim was disputed by William, who insisted that Edward had promised him the throne. Only weeks before the battle, Harold had marched north to defeat a Norwegian invasion led by Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge near York. He then hurried south to confront the Normans, who had landed at Pevensey on the Sussex coast. The English fought on foot behind a shield wall on Senlac Hill, while William relied on a combination of archers, infantry and mounted knights. The fighting lasted most of the day. Feigned retreats by the Norman cavalry may have drawn parts of the English line down the slope, and late in the afternoon Harold was killed, traditionally by an arrow to the eye, although the story is debated. William was crowned at Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day and spent the following years suppressing rebellions. The battle is famously depicted in the Bayeux Tapestry, an embroidered cloth nearly seventy metres long, and the town of Battle grew up around the abbey William founded on the site.

question: In what year did the storming of the Bastille take place?
document: The storming of the Bastille took place on 14 July, when crowds in Paris attacked the medieval fortress on the eastern edge of the city. The Bastille had long served as a state prison, and to many Parisians it symbolized the arbitrary power of the monarchy under Louis XVI. Tension in the capital had been building for weeks. The Estates-General had opened at Versailles in May, and in June the deputies of the Third Estate declared themselves a National Assembly and swore the Tennis Court Oath, promising not to disband until France had a constitution. When the king dismissed the popular finance minister Jacques Necker and royal troops gathered around Paris, rumors spread that the Assembly would be crushed. On the morning of the attack, crowds seized tens of thousands of muskets from the Invalides and then marched on the Bastille in search of gunpowder. The governor, Bernard-René de Launay, eventually surrendered after several hours of fighting, during which about a hundred attackers were killed. De Launay was then murdered, and his head was paraded through the streets on a pike. Only seven prisoners were found inside. The fortress was demolished over the following months, and some of its stones were carved into souvenir models. The anniversary of the attack is now celebrated as France's national holiday.
rationale: The passage gives the day, month, and surrounding revolutionary events but never the year 1789, so a correct answer requires recalled knowledge.

question: In what year was the Battle of Waterloo fought?
document: The Battle of Waterloo was fought on 18 June near the village of Waterloo, south of Brussels in what is now Belgium. It pitted Napoleon Bonaparte, who had escaped from exile on the island of Elba and returned to power in France, against two allied armies: an Anglo-allied force commanded by the Duke of Wellington and a Prussian army under Field Marshal Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher. Two days earlier, Napoleon had defeated the Prussians at Ligny, but Blücher's army withdrew in good order rather than retreating eastward, which allowed it to march to Wellington's aid. On the day of the battle, heavy overnight rain delayed the French attack until late morning. Wellington's troops held a ridge and defended the farmhouses of Hougoumont and La Haye Sainte against repeated assaults, including massed French cavalry charges against infantry squares. In the evening, as Prussian columns pressed on the French right flank at Plancenoit, Napoleon committed the Imperial Guard, whose repulse caused the French army to collapse. Wellington later called the battle the nearest-run thing you ever saw in your life. Napoleon abdicated for the second time a few days later and was exiled to the remote island of Saint Helena in the South Atlantic.
rationale: The document narrates the battle and its aftermath without stating 1815 or any relative date that would let the year be derived.

question: In which Virginia village did Robert E. Lee surrender to Ulysses S. Grant in April 1865?
document: By the spring, the Confederate Army of Northern Virginia was in desperate condition. After a long siege, Union forces under Ulysses S. Grant broke through the defenses of Petersburg on 2 April, forcing Robert E. Lee to abandon both Petersburg and the Confederate capital of Richmond. Lee led his starving army west, hoping to reach supplies by rail and then turn south to join General Joseph E. Johnston's forces in North Carolina. Union cavalry under Philip Sheridan raced ahead and captured the waiting supply trains, and at Sailor's Creek on 6 April several thousand of Lee's men were cut off and captured. After an exchange of letters, Lee met Grant on 9 April in the parlor of a brick house owned by Wilmer McLean, who, by a strange coincidence, had moved there after his previous home near Manassas was caught up in the first major battle of the war. Grant offered generous terms: Confederate soldiers would be paroled and allowed to go home, officers could keep their sidearms, and men who claimed horses or mules could take them back to work their farms. Three days later, the Confederate infantry formally stacked their arms in a ceremony overseen by Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain. Although other Confederate forces remained in the field for several more weeks, the surrender is widely regarded as the effective end of the American Civil War.

question: Which treaty, signed in June 1919, formally ended the First World War between Germany and the Allied Powers?
document: After the armistice of November 1918 halted the fighting on the Western Front, the victorious Allies gathered in Paris to negotiate the peace. The conference was dominated by the so-called Big Four: Woodrow Wilson of the United States, David Lloyd George of Britain, Georges Clemenceau of France, and Vittorio Orlando of Italy. Germany was not invited to take part in the negotiations and was presented with the finished terms, which its delegates denounced as a dictated peace. The settlement required Germany to return Alsace-Lorraine to France, give up its overseas colonies, and cede territory to Belgium, Denmark, and the newly re-created Polish state, including a corridor to the Baltic Sea that separated East Prussia from the rest of the country. The Rhineland was to be demilitarized and occupied by Allied troops, the German army was limited to one hundred thousand men, and the country was forbidden to have an air force or submarines. Article 231, often called the war guilt clause, held Germany and its allies responsible for the loss and damage caused by the war and served as the basis for heavy reparations. The agreement also contained the covenant establishing the League of Nations, although the United States Senate refused to ratify it. Many historians argue that German resentment of its terms contributed to the political instability that followed.

question: What 1494 treaty divided newly discovered lands outside Europe between Spain and Portugal along a north-south line in the Atlantic?
document: Christopher Columbus's return from his first voyage across the Atlantic set off a diplomatic dispute between the crowns of Castile and Portugal. The Portuguese king, John II, argued that the newly found islands fell within the sphere already granted to Portugal by earlier agreements and papal bulls, while Ferdinand and Isabella insisted they belonged to Spain. In response to Spanish lobbying, Pope Alexander VI, himself a Spaniard, issued the bull Inter caetera, which drew a line of demarcation one hundred leagues west of the Azores and Cape Verde islands and assigned lands beyond it to Spain. Unhappy with this arrangement, the Portuguese negotiated directly with the Spanish monarchs. The resulting agreement moved the dividing meridian to a point 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands. Lands to the east of the line were reserved for Portugal, and lands to the west for Spain. Because the new line cut across the eastern bulge of South America, it later gave Portugal its claim to Brazil, which Pedro Álvares Cabral reached in 1500. Other European powers, notably England, France, and the Netherlands, never recognized the division. A later agreement, the Treaty of Zaragoza, attempted to fix a corresponding line on the opposite side of the world to settle rival claims in the Spice Islands.
rationale: The passage explains the dispute and the 370-league line but never names Tordesillas (only the later Treaty of Zaragoza, which is a wrong answer), so the correct name requires memory.

question: Which Portuguese navigator commanded the first European voyage to reach India by sailing around Africa, arriving in 1498?
document: Portugal's search for a sea route to Asia had been building for most of the fifteenth century. Under the patronage of Prince Henry the Navigator, Portuguese captains pushed steadily down the west coast of Africa, and in 1488 Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip of the continent, proving that the Atlantic connected to the Indian Ocean. King Manuel I then commissioned a fleet of four ships to complete the journey. The expedition left Lisbon in July 1497 and, instead of hugging the African coast, swung far out into the South Atlantic to catch favorable winds, spending about three months out of sight of land. After rounding the Cape of Good Hope, the fleet worked its way up the east African coast, meeting hostility at Mozambique and Mombasa but finding a friendly reception at Malindi, where it took on a pilot familiar with the monsoon routes. The ships crossed the Arabian Sea and anchored near Calicut on the Malabar Coast. Negotiations with the local ruler, the Zamorin, were strained, partly because the Portuguese gifts seemed paltry to a court accustomed to rich trade. The return voyage was grueling; scurvy killed many of the crew, and only two ships made it back to Lisbon. Even so, the cargo of spices was enough to show the immense profits the new route could bring.

question: Which Portuguese-born navigator commanded the Spanish fleet that set out in 1519 on the expedition that completed the first circumnavigation of the globe?
document: The expedition sailed from Sanlúcar de Barrameda with five ships and roughly 270 men, financed by the Spanish crown under the young King Charles I, who hoped to reach the Spice Islands by sailing west. The voyage was troubled from the start. A mutiny among the Spanish captains was put down during the winter at Port San Julián in Patagonia, and one ship was wrecked while scouting the coast. In late 1520 the fleet found and threaded a narrow, winding passage near the southern tip of South America, losing another ship whose crew deserted and turned back to Spain. The remaining vessels emerged into a vast ocean so calm that they named it the Pacific. The crossing took more than three months, and the crew survived on biscuit crumbs, foul water, sawdust, and leather. In the Philippines the commander became involved in local rivalries and was killed at the Battle of Mactan in April 1521 by warriors loyal to the chieftain Lapulapu. The survivors burned one ship for lack of crew and eventually reached the Moluccas. Only the Victoria, captained by Juan Sebastián Elcano, completed the return voyage around the Cape of Good Hope, arriving in Spain in September 1522 with eighteen men. The journal of the Italian chronicler Antonio Pigafetta remains the main eyewitness account.

question: Which Carthaginian general led an army with war elephants across the Alps to invade Italy during the Second Punic War?
document: The Second Punic War broke out after Carthaginian forces besieged and captured Saguntum, a city in Spain allied with Rome. Rather than wait for Rome to strike at Carthage's Spanish holdings or at Africa itself, the Carthaginian commander chose to carry the war into Italy by land. Leaving New Carthage in the spring of 218 BC with a large army of infantry, cavalry and several dozen war elephants, he crossed the Ebro, fought his way through the Pyrenees, and forded the Rhône despite opposition from local Gallic tribes. The crossing of the Alps in autumn was the most famous part of the campaign. Snow, narrow paths, landslides and attacks by mountain tribes cost him a large part of his army, and most of the elephants did not survive the following winter. Once in northern Italy, however, he won a series of crushing victories, first at the Trebia, then at Lake Trasimene, where a Roman army was ambushed in the fog, and finally at Cannae in 216 BC, where a double envelopment destroyed one of the largest armies Rome had ever fielded. Despite these triumphs, he could not force Rome to surrender, and many of its Italian allies remained loyal. Rome adopted the delaying tactics associated with Quintus Fabius Maximus, and the war was eventually decided in Africa, where Scipio Africanus defeated the Carthaginians at Zama in 202 BC.
rationale: The passage describes the Alpine crossing and the general's victories while referring only to 'the Carthaginian commander', never naming him or his family, so the answer requires memory.

question: Which leader founded the Mongol Empire, uniting the Mongol tribes in the early thirteenth century?
document: The founder of the Mongol Empire was born on the Mongolian steppe, probably in the 1160s, into a minor aristocratic family. His father, a chieftain, was poisoned by rival Tatars when the boy was still young, and the family was abandoned by its followers, surviving for a time by fishing and gathering roots. Through a combination of personal alliances, military talent and ruthless treatment of rivals, he gradually rose to dominate the tribes of the steppe, defeating the Tatars, the Keraites, the Naimans and his former sworn brother Jamukha. In 1206 a great assembly, or kurultai, held near the Onon River proclaimed him supreme ruler of all the Mongols. He reorganized his followers into decimal units of tens, hundreds and thousands, deliberately breaking up old tribal loyalties, and promoted commanders on merit. He also introduced a code of laws and adopted a script borrowed from the Uyghurs. His armies, built around highly mobile horse archers, then turned outward, attacking the Western Xia, the Jin dynasty of northern China, and the Khwarazmian Empire in Central Asia, where cities such as Bukhara, Samarkand and Merv suffered terrible destruction. He died in 1227 during a campaign against the Western Xia, and his empire was divided among his sons and grandsons, who extended it even further.

question: Who served as the first Chancellor of the German Empire after its unification in 1871?
document: The German Empire was proclaimed on 18 January 1871 at a ceremony held in occupied France, while the Franco-Prussian War was still drawing to a close and Paris remained under siege. King Wilhelm I of Prussia was declared German Emperor, and the southern German states of Bavaria, Württemberg, Baden and Hesse joined the North German Confederation to form a single federal state dominated by Prussia. Unification had been achieved through three short wars: against Denmark in 1864, against Austria in 1866, and against France in 1870 and 1871. The Prussian minister-president who had steered these conflicts became the head of the new imperial government. In domestic affairs his government waged the Kulturkampf against the political influence of the Catholic Church, passed anti-socialist laws, and at the same time introduced pioneering social insurance programs covering sickness, accidents, old age and disability. In foreign policy he sought to isolate France and keep the peace among the great powers through a complex web of alliances, including the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary and the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia. He also hosted the Congress of Berlin in 1878, which redrew the map of the Balkans. After the young Wilhelm II came to the throne, the two men clashed over policy, and the chancellor was forced to resign in 1890.

question: What was the name of the ship that carried the Pilgrims from England to Plymouth, Massachusetts, in 1620?
document: The group later known as the Pilgrims was made up largely of English Separatists, Protestants who had broken away from the Church of England and who had spent more than a decade living in exile in the Dutch city of Leiden. Worried that their children were losing their English identity, they arranged financing from a group of London merchant investors and obtained permission to settle in the territory of the Virginia Company. They originally planned to sail in two vessels, but the smaller ship, the Speedwell, leaked so badly that it had to be abandoned after two false starts, and the passengers were crowded onto a single ship that finally left Plymouth, England, in September. Only some of the 102 passengers were Separatists; the rest were hired craftsmen, servants and other settlers whom the Pilgrims called Strangers. After a rough crossing of some sixty-six days, they sighted Cape Cod in November, far north of their intended destination. Because they were outside the area covered by their patent, forty-one adult men signed a short agreement pledging to form a civil body politic and obey laws made for the general good. The settlers chose a site at Plymouth harbor in December. During the first winter, many continued to live aboard the ship, and roughly half of the colonists died of disease and exposure. The ship sailed back to England in April 1621.

question: Who was the first emperor of a unified China, founding the Qin dynasty in 221 BC?
document: The state of Qin, located in the Wei River valley of northwestern China, rose to dominance during the Warring States period through a series of harsh but effective reforms associated with the statesman Shang Yang, which rewarded military merit and agricultural production and weakened the old aristocracy. Its young king came to the throne as a boy and assumed personal power in his early twenties. In a rapid series of campaigns lasting about a decade, Qin armies conquered the six rival states of Han, Zhao, Wei, Chu, Yan and Qi. After the conquest, the ruler adopted a new title meant to elevate him above the kings of the past, and with his chancellor Li Si he set about imposing uniformity on the realm. Weights, measures, coinage, axle widths and the written script were standardized, the old feudal territories were replaced by commanderies governed by appointed officials, and existing defensive walls in the north were linked into an early version of the Great Wall. The regime also became notorious for the burning of books and, according to later historians, the execution of scholars. The ruler made long tours of inspection and grew obsessed with finding an elixir of immortality. He died in 210 BC while traveling in the east, and his dynasty collapsed only four years later. His vast tomb complex near modern Xi'an, guarded by thousands of life-sized terracotta soldiers, was discovered by farmers digging a well in 1974.

question: Which Scottish scientist discovered penicillin?
document: Penicillin is often described as the drug that opened the antibiotic era. The substance is produced by a mould of the genus Penicillium, and its antibacterial effect was first noticed when a culture plate of Staphylococcus bacteria, left on a laboratory bench in London, became contaminated by a stray mould spore. Around the mould colony the bacteria had died back, leaving a clear ring. The observation was published in a medical journal in 1929, but for nearly a decade little came of it, because the active compound was unstable and difficult to purify in useful amounts. The breakthrough toward a usable medicine came at the University of Oxford, where Howard Florey and Ernst Chain led a team that extracted and concentrated the drug at the end of the 1930s. Norman Heatley devised many of the improvised extraction methods, using bedpans, milk churns and bathtubs as equipment. In 1941 the first patient, a local policeman, was treated; he improved dramatically before supplies ran out. During the Second World War, American companies developed deep-tank fermentation, and by D-Day enough penicillin existed to treat Allied casualties on a large scale. The 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine recognized the work.

question: Which astronomer formulated the three laws of planetary motion, including the law that planets travel in elliptical orbits?
document: The three laws of planetary motion transformed astronomy in the early seventeenth century. The first states that each planet moves along an ellipse, with the Sun at one of the two foci, rather than on the perfect circles that had dominated cosmology since antiquity. The second holds that a line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time, meaning that a planet moves faster when it is nearer the Sun and slower when it is farther away. The third, published about a decade after the first two, relates the square of a planet's orbital period to the cube of its average distance from the Sun. The laws were derived from painstaking naked-eye observations of Mars and the other planets, gathered over many years at the observatory of Uraniborg on the island of Hven. Mars proved especially important, because its orbit is noticeably eccentric and stubbornly refused to fit a circular model. The laws were empirical: they described how planets move without explaining why. That explanation came later in the century, when Isaac Newton showed that all three could be derived from a single inverse-square law of gravitation. Today the same relationships are used to estimate the masses of stars that host exoplanets.
rationale: The passage explains all three laws and their observational basis without naming the astronomer who formulated them, so the answer is memory-only.

question: On which planet is the Great Red Spot, a giant long-lived anticyclonic storm, located?
document: The Great Red Spot is the best-known storm in the solar system. It is a high-pressure system, an anticyclone, that rotates counterclockwise in the planet's southern hemisphere, wedged in a band of clouds between opposing jet streams. Observers have tracked the current spot continuously since the 1830s, and some historians argue that a spot recorded by Giovanni Cassini in the 1660s may have been the same feature, although a long gap in observations makes the link uncertain. The storm's winds reach several hundred kilometres per hour near its edges, while the centre is comparatively calm. Measurements over the past century and a half show that the spot is shrinking. In the late nineteenth century it was estimated to be roughly forty thousand kilometres across; it has since contracted to well under half that width, though it remains wider than Earth. Its colour, which ranges from brick red to pale salmon, is still not fully explained; one leading idea is that sunlight breaks apart chemicals such as ammonia and acetylene high in the atmosphere, producing reddish compounds. Microwave measurements from an orbiting spacecraft have revealed that the storm's roots extend hundreds of kilometres below the visible cloud tops.

question: In what year did the Soviet Union launch Sputnik 1, the first artificial Earth satellite?
document: Sputnik 1 was a polished metal sphere about 58 centimetres in diameter, fitted with four long whip antennas that trailed behind it like whiskers. It weighed roughly 84 kilograms and carried two radio transmitters, which broadcast a simple series of beeps on frequencies of about 20 and 40 megahertz. Amateur radio operators around the world could pick up the signal, and newspapers printed instructions for listening to it. The satellite was launched from the Baikonur site in Soviet Kazakhstan on an R-7 rocket, originally designed as an intercontinental ballistic missile, under the direction of chief designer Sergei Korolev. It travelled in a low elliptical orbit, circling the planet about once every 96 minutes. Its batteries lasted around three weeks, after which the transmitters fell silent, and the sphere itself burned up on re-entry roughly three months after launch. The political effect was far larger than the scientific payload. In the United States the launch provoked alarm about a missile gap, accelerated the creation of NASA, and led to new federal spending on science education. About a month later the Soviets followed with a second, much heavier satellite that carried a dog named Laika.

question: Which German physicist discovered X-rays in 1895?
document: X-rays were discovered by accident in a darkened laboratory at the University of Würzburg late in the nineteenth century. While experimenting with a cathode-ray tube wrapped in black cardboard, the physicist noticed that a screen coated with barium platinocyanide, lying some distance away, began to glow. Because the tube was fully covered, ordinary light could not explain the effect. Over the following weeks the work continued almost in secret, as the researcher tested which materials the new rays could pass through. Paper, wood and thin sheets of aluminium were largely transparent, whereas lead stopped the rays almost completely. The name X-rays was chosen to signal their unknown nature. The most famous image from this period shows the bones of a woman's hand, with a ring visible on one finger, recorded on a photographic plate. Within months of the announcement, doctors across Europe and North America were using the rays to locate bullets and examine fractures. The dangers took longer to appreciate, and many early operators suffered burns and, later, cancers. The discovery earned the very first Nobel Prize in Physics, awarded in 1901.

question: Which Russian chemist published a periodic table in 1869 that left gaps for undiscovered elements?
document: The periodic table emerged in the 1860s, when several chemists were trying to find order among the roughly sixty elements then known. Britain's John Newlands proposed a law of octaves, noting that similar properties seemed to recur every eighth element when they were listed by atomic weight, but his idea was ridiculed at the Chemical Society. In Germany, Lothar Meyer developed a table based on atomic volumes. The version that won the most lasting recognition was drawn up by a professor at St Petersburg University while he was writing a chemistry textbook. Its decisive feature was boldness: rather than force every known element into the next available slot, it left empty spaces and predicted that undiscovered elements would fill them. The table even forecast the approximate atomic weights, densities and oxides of these missing elements, which were provisionally called eka-aluminium, eka-boron and eka-silicon. When gallium was isolated in 1875, followed by scandium in 1879 and germanium in 1886, their properties closely matched the predictions, and sceptics were won over. The table was later reorganised by atomic number rather than atomic weight after Henry Moseley's X-ray work in 1913, which resolved awkward placements such as tellurium and iodine.
rationale: The passage discusses rival tables and the predictive success of the 1869 table but never names its author or the element named after him.

question: Which Scottish engineer invented the separate condenser that greatly improved the efficiency of the steam engine?
document: Before the separate condenser, the dominant steam engine was the atmospheric engine designed by Thomas Newcomen in the early eighteenth century and used mainly to pump water out of mines. In that design, steam filled a cylinder and was then condensed by a spray of cold water inside the same cylinder, creating a partial vacuum so that atmospheric pressure pushed the piston down. The method was enormously wasteful, because the cylinder had to be reheated with fresh steam after every stroke. The decisive insight came in 1765, reportedly during a Sunday walk on Glasgow Green, after a model Newcomen engine had been brought in for repair at the University of Glasgow. The solution was to condense the steam in a separate vessel, kept permanently cold, while the main cylinder stayed hot. Fuel consumption fell by roughly three quarters. Turning the idea into reliable machinery took years. A partnership with the Birmingham manufacturer Matthew Boulton supplied capital and skilled workers, and John Wilkinson's precise cylinder-boring technique made it possible to build tight-fitting pistons. Later refinements included the sun-and-planet gear, which converted reciprocating motion into rotary motion, and the centrifugal governor for regulating engine speed.
rationale: The passage explains the separate condenser and its development in detail without naming the inventor or mentioning the unit of power named after him.

question: How many bones are in the typical adult human skeleton?
document: The human skeleton changes considerably over a lifetime. A newborn has somewhere around 270 to 300 separate bony elements, many of them still partly made of cartilage. As a child grows, a number of these pieces fuse together. The skull is a clear example: at birth its plates are separated by flexible seams and soft spots called fontanelles, which allow the head to compress slightly during delivery and leave room for the rapidly growing brain. Over the first two years these gaps close. Similarly, the sacrum at the base of the spine begins as five separate vertebrae that fuse during adolescence and early adulthood, and each hip bone forms from the union of the ilium, ischium and pubis. Long bones such as the femur grow at cartilage plates near their ends, which ossify once growth is complete, usually by the early twenties. The femur is the longest and strongest bone in the body, while the stapes in the middle ear is the smallest, about three millimetres long. More than half of the skeleton's bones are found in the hands and feet. The exact adult count varies a little between individuals because of extra sesamoid bones, an additional rib, or unfused vertebrae.
rationale: The passage gives the newborn bone count and describes fusion but never states the standard adult total, which must come from memory.

question: Deficiency of which vitamin causes scurvy?
document: Scurvy was once among the most feared diseases of long sea voyages. Its early signs are fatigue and aching limbs, followed by swollen, bleeding gums, loosened teeth, easy bruising and the reopening of old wounds, because the body can no longer maintain the collagen that holds tissues together. Left untreated, it is fatal. During the age of sail, scurvy is thought to have killed more sailors than storms, battles and shipwreck combined; on George Anson's circumnavigation in the 1740s, most of the crew died, largely of the disease. In 1747 the Scottish naval surgeon James Lind carried out one of the earliest controlled clinical trials aboard HMS Salisbury, dividing twelve sick sailors into pairs and giving each pair a different remedy, such as cider, vinegar, sea water or citrus fruit. The pair given oranges and lemons recovered strikingly fast. Even so, the Royal Navy did not make lemon juice a standard ration until 1795. Confusion persisted into the twentieth century, partly because limes, later substituted for lemons, were less effective. Humans, along with guinea pigs and certain other primates, cannot synthesize the protective nutrient themselves. The Hungarian biochemist Albert Szent-Györgyi isolated the compound around 1930 and later received a Nobel Prize for his work.
rationale: The passage covers scurvy's symptoms, Lind's citrus trial and the nutrient's isolation without ever naming the vitamin or its chemical name.

question: Which British computer scientist invented the World Wide Web while working at CERN?
document: The World Wide Web began as an internal proposal at CERN, the European particle physics laboratory near Geneva. In March 1989 a memo titled Information Management: A Proposal described a system of linked documents that would let researchers at different institutions share information without needing to know where it was stored. A supervisor famously scribbled the words vague but exciting on the cover. By late 1990 the core pieces were running: the HyperText Markup Language for writing pages, the Hypertext Transfer Protocol for moving them across the network, and the uniform resource locator for addressing them. question: Which English physicist discovered the neutron in 1932?
document: The neutron completed the basic picture of the atomic nucleus. By the 1920s physicists knew that nuclei contained protons, but the masses of most atoms were roughly twice what their protons alone could account for. Ernest Rutherford speculated as early as 1920 that a neutral particle might exist inside the nucleus, yet detecting something with no electric charge was extremely difficult. Important clues came from Germany and France. Walther Bothe and Herbert Becker found that bombarding beryllium with alpha particles produced a highly penetrating radiation, which they assumed was a form of gamma ray. Irène Joliot-Curie and Frédéric Joliot then showed that this radiation could knock protons out of paraffin wax at high speed. At the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, a longtime colleague of Rutherford repeated and extended these experiments, measuring the recoil of nuclei of several different elements. The results were incompatible with gamma rays but fitted neatly if the radiation consisted of uncharged particles with a mass close to that of the proton. The finding was announced in a brief letter to Nature titled Possible Existence of a Neutron. It earned the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1935, and within a few years neutrons were being used to split heavy nuclei.

question: Which mineral ranks as the hardest, at 10, on the Mohs scale of mineral hardness?
document: The Mohs scale of mineral hardness was devised in 1812 by the German geologist and mineralogist Friedrich Mohs. It is an ordinal scale based on scratch resistance: a mineral can scratch any mineral ranked below it but is scratched by those ranked above it. Mohs chose ten reference minerals that were readily available. At the soft end sits talc, which can be scratched with a fingernail, followed by gypsum and then calcite. Fluorite occupies the fourth position, apatite the fifth, and orthoclase feldspar the sixth. Quartz, at seven, is hard enough to scratch ordinary glass, which makes it a useful field test. Topaz is rated eight, and corundum, the mineral family that includes ruby and sapphire, is rated nine. Because the scale is ordinal, the intervals between steps are uneven; the gap between nine and ten is far larger in absolute hardness than the gap between one and nine. Field geologists still carry simple kits for quick tests: a fingernail rates about 2.5, a copper coin about 3.5, a steel knife blade about 5.5, and a glass plate about 5.5 to 6. More precise instruments, such as the Vickers and Knoop indentation tests, are used when exact measurements are needed.

question: What is the most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere by volume?
document: Earth's atmosphere is a mixture of gases held close to the planet by gravity. Oxygen, produced over billions of years by photosynthesis, makes up roughly 21 percent of dry air by volume. Argon, a noble gas released by the radioactive decay of potassium in rocks, accounts for a little under one percent. Carbon dioxide, though present at only about 420 parts per million, plays an outsized role in regulating climate because it absorbs infrared radiation. Trace gases include neon, helium, methane, krypton, hydrogen and ozone. Water vapour is usually excluded from figures for dry air because its concentration varies widely, from almost nothing over polar deserts to around four percent in humid tropical air. Roughly three quarters of the atmosphere's total mass lies within the lowest layer, the troposphere, where weather occurs. Above it, the stratosphere contains the ozone layer, which absorbs much of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet light. The proportions of the major gases are remarkably uniform up to about 80 kilometres, because turbulent mixing keeps them evenly blended. Higher still, lighter gases begin to separate out according to their molecular mass, and atomic oxygen becomes increasingly important.

question: What is the SI unit of frequency, equal to one cycle per second?
document: Frequency describes how often a repeating event occurs in a given span of time. For a wave, it is the number of complete oscillations that pass a fixed point each second, and it is inversely related to the period, the time taken for a single cycle. A pendulum that completes one swing back and forth every two seconds has a frequency of one half cycle per second. Frequency and wavelength are linked through the speed of the wave: for light in a vacuum, multiplying the two always gives the same constant, so higher-frequency light has shorter wavelengths. The SI unit of frequency was adopted by the General Conference on Weights and Measures in 1960, replacing the older expression cycles per second, which had been common in engineering and radio. Everyday examples span an enormous range. Mains electricity alternates fifty or sixty times a second depending on the country, and concert pitch A is tuned to 440 cycles per second. FM radio stations broadcast at around a hundred million cycles per second, while visible light oscillates hundreds of trillions of times each second. Angular frequency, used widely in physics, is measured instead in radians per second.
rationale: The passage defines frequency and mentions the adoption of its SI unit without ever naming the unit or its symbol.

question: In what year was Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species first published?

Back in England, he filled notebooks with speculations about the transmutation of species and, after reading Thomas Malthus on population, hit upon the mechanism of selection. For years he hesitated to publish, accumulating evidence from pigeon breeding, barnacle anatomy and correspondence with naturalists worldwide. His hand was forced when Alfred Russel Wallace, working in the Malay Archipelago, sent him an essay outlining nearly the same theory. A joint presentation of their work was arranged at the Linnean Society of London, and Darwin then hurried to condense his planned big species book into a single volume. The publisher was John Murray, and the first printing of about 1,250 copies was taken up by booksellers on the day of release.
